title: Tatpuruṣāya vidmahe: the fourth of the five ‘brahma’ mantras
theme: A gāyatrī to Tatpuruṣa, ‘that Person’, the eastern face, by the commentators’ account: we know him, we meditate on him, may he impel us.

words.context: Sāyaṇa: «द्वितीयार्थे चतुर्थी» — the dative is used for the accusative
Sāyaṇa: «विद्महे गुरुशास्त्रमुखाज्जानीमः» — we know through the teacher and the scripture
Sāyaṇa: «तत्तस्मात्कारणाद्रुद्रो देवो» — for that reason, the god Rudra

sandhi.type: t before a nasal; -aḥ before a voiced sound
sandhi.rule: tat + naḥ → tan no: t becomes n before n (P. 8.4.45 (यरोऽनुनासिकेऽनुनासिको वा)); naḥ becomes no before r.

morphology.note: The dative stands where an accusative is meant (‘we know Tatpuruṣa’), as Sāyaṇa says; the same holds for mahādevāya. This is the regular form of the gāyatrīs of this Upaniṣad.
A subjunctive (leṭ) with the augment a, as Bhāskara notes (लेट्याडागमः): ‘may he impel’. Bhāskara explains tatpuruṣāya by a dropped dative ending of tad: «तदिति चतुर्थ्या लुक्».

translation.literal: [To] Tatpuruṣa we know, [to] the Great God may we meditate; therefore may Rudra impel us.
translation.readable: We know Tatpuruṣa; we meditate on the Great God. So may Rudra urge us on.

anvaya: तत्पुरुषाय विद्महे महादेवाय धीमहि । तत् रुद्रः नः प्रचोदयात् ।
syntax: Two first-person plural verbs, vidmahe and dhīmahi, each with its object in the dative, followed by a third-person wish (pracodayāt) with Rudra as subject and naḥ as object. The form is that of the gāyatrī: know, meditate, may he impel.

ambiguities.note: Sāyaṇa takes tat as ‘therefore’; Bhāskara, in his first anuvāka, takes it as ‘there’, «अथ तत् तत्र नो ऽस्मान् रुद्रः».

metre.name: gāyatrī
metre.note: Three pādas of eight syllables (tatpuruṣāya vidmahe · mahādevāya dhīmahi · tan no rudraḥ pracodayāt), printed in two lines of 16 and 8.

beginner: This is the fourth of the five ‘brahma’ mantras to the faces of Śiva, and it has the shape of the famous Gāyatrī: ‘we know …, we meditate on …, may he urge us on’. Here the one known is Tatpuruṣa, ‘that Person’, whom the old commentators identify with the eastern face; the one meditated on is the Great God; and the one asked to inspire is Rudra. Sāyaṇa explains the order: first we come to know him from a teacher and the scriptures, then we meditate on what we know, and so we ask him to move us toward knowledge and meditation. The Upaniṣad uses the same three-step form for many deities, and the first anuvāka of this text already contains this very gāyatrī.
analogy: Like a student’s three steps with a great teacher: learn who they are, keep them in mind, and ask to be set in motion.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: We know Tatpuruṣa, we meditate on the Great God; may Rudra impel us.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa: the mantra of the eastern face, whose god is named Tatpuruṣa. Sāyaṇa: «प्राग्वक्त्रेदेवस्तत्पुरुषनामकः».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa: we know him from the mouth of teacher and scripture, then meditate on him, and therefore ask Rudra to impel us toward knowledge and meditation: «विद्महे गुरुशास्त्रमुखाज्जानीमः। ज्ञात्वा च महादेवाय तं महादेवं धीमहि ध्यायेम», and «नोऽस्मान्प्रचोदयाज्ज्ञानध्यानार्थं प्रेरयतु».

commentary.q: Why does Bhāskara not explain it here?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: He says it was explained at ‘ambhasy apāre’, the first anuvāka, where the same gāyatrī stands among others: «तत्पुरुषायेति व्याख्यातं» — at ambhasy apāre. There he calls it the first of five gāyatrīs used in the worship of the Lord, «तत्पुरुषायेत्याद्याः पञ्च गायत्र्यः», and here adds that some part of the god pervading Rudra is meant: «अत्रापि पुरुषेश्वर रुद्रव्यापको देवांशः कश्चित्प्रतिपाद्यः».

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this text is in the edition’s sources (Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not available here). The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa agree word for word; Bhāskara refers back to his first anuvāka.

contemporary.text: Know, then reflect, then ask to be moved: the order of the mantra is also an order of learning anything well. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: What is the difference between knowing about something and keeping it in mind?
reflect.deeper: The gāyatrī form recurs for many deities. What does a shared form suggest about how the tradition thought of them?
reflect.practice: Choose one idea you have learned this week and spend two quiet minutes with it.

references.text: The same gāyatrī stands in anuvāka 10.1 among the gāyatrīs of the deities; Bhāskara comments on it there. This is Sāyaṇa’s and Bhāskara’s anuvāka 46.
The form follows the Sāvitrī (RV 3.62.10, tat savitur vareṇyam … dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt); the edition’s Ṛgveda source has only maṇḍala 1, so it is not cited as a checked parallel.

flags.note: The identification with the eastern face is the commentators’; the text names Tatpuruṣa, Mahādeva and Rudra.
